newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FORECAST-Australia jobless to remain above 8.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Australia jobless to remain above 8.5 pct.

text.p: Australia's labour market is not showing any signs of improvement because, even though employment is expected post a large increase in April, the unemployment rate is seen remaining above 8.5 percent.
Employment is one of the weakest areas of the economy, and has been since mid-1995, but analysts and the government remain optimistic that there will be improvement later this year.
The median forecast of the 27 economists Reuters surveyed is for a rise in employment of 35,000 in April. Forecasts range from a fall of 5,000 to a rise of 60,000.

While that appears a strong rise, it follows total job losses of 40,900 in the previous two months. Indeed, it would mean that over the previous 12 months, employment would have grown by about 130,000 -- or about 10,800 new jobs a month.
"We expect a correction to the negative outcomes over the last couple of months but employment growth is trending only weakly up," Dresdner chief economist Rob Henderson said.
And employment growth that has occurred has been almost exclusively in part-time jobs -- over the year to March full-time jobs fell by 6,000, while part-time positions were up 96,100.
"The softer conditions in the labour market over the last few months appear to be fairly broadly based," Akis Haralabopoulos said.
Reflecting the stagnant underlying nature of the jobs market, the unemployment rate is seen unchanged in April at 8.7 percent despite the expected employment rise.

When the Reserve Bank of Australia announced the first interest rate cut in three years on July 31 last year, it said the stalling of the unemployment rate around 8.5 percent over the previous year had been a factor in its decision.
The high unemployment rate was also a supporting factor in the decision to lower rates in November and December.

But despite the easier policy, unemployment has shown no improvement -- between January and July 1996 it ranged between 8.3 and 8.8 percent while since August it has ranged between 8.5 and 8.8 percent.

However, economists said that while the employment data was a concern, it was a lagging indicator of activity and therefore reflecting weakness in the second half of 1996, while the outlook was more positive.

"We expect the economy to strengthen over the course of 1997 as the interest rates cuts of 1996 continue to flow through," Hambros fixed income economist Su-Lin Ong said, with the rate cuts seen helping housing, consumer spending and investment.
"As suggested by the leading indicators of the labour market, employment growth is likely to improve modestly in coming months and strengthen further into 1997," she said.
One leading indicator backing this was Monday's ANZ job advertisement series showing a record 16.7 percent rise.

The data was affected by the fact Easter fell entirely in March, something which may also bias the employment data to the upside, but even without the the Easter effect, job ads would have been up around five percent, the ANZ said.
This was still seen as a fairly strong rise, and a positive for employment prospects later in the year.
Treasurer Peter Costello was positive on the employment outlook even before the job ads series came out.

"I think throughout the course of 1997 and 1998 the pace of economic activity is going to pick up, and I expect the pace of employment growth to pick up," Costello said in a television interview last Sunday.
"The good news is more jobs."
The Statistics Bureau will release the jobs date at 0130 GMT (11.30 a.m.) on Thursday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
